knowledge-base.overview: Official C# coding conventions and .NET best practices that go beyond the guardrails in lang-csharp.xml. Covers naming rules, var usage, async patterns in library vs application code, DI anti-patterns, and EF Core query performance. Loaded alongside lang-csharp.xml for .cs and .csproj files.

naming-conventions.description: Official .NET naming rules from Microsoft and the runtime repo. These apply to all new code regardless of framework.

rules.rule: PascalCase for types (classes, structs, records, enums, interfaces), public and protected members (methods, properties, events, fields), and constants: `MaxRetryCount`, `UserService`, `IUserRepository`
_camelCase for private and internal fields: `_userId`, `_logger`, `_connectionString`. The underscore prefix marks the field as instance state at a glance.
camelCase for parameters and local variables: `userId`, `cancellationToken`, `itemCount`
ALL_CAPS is NOT used in .NET. Constants use PascalCase: `MaxRetryCount`, not `MAX_RETRY_COUNT`
Interfaces always start with I: `IUserRepository`, `IOrderService`
Async methods always end with Async: `GetUserAsync`, `SaveOrderAsync`. Non-async methods must NOT end with Async.
Avoid Hungarian notation and type-encoding in names: `strName` and `intCount` are wrong; use `name` and `count`
Acronyms of two letters stay uppercase (IO, UI, DB); three or more use PascalCase (Html, Xml, Http)

var-usage.description: When to use var vs explicit types. The rule: use var when the type is obvious from the right side of the assignment, without needing to read documentation or hover over the identifier.

rules.rule: Use var when the type is immediately visible: `var user = new User()`, `var users = new List<User>()`
Use var for LINQ queries and anonymous types — you have no choice and explicit types are harder to read
Use var for loop variables in for loops: `for (var i = 0; i < count; i++)`
Use explicit types when the type is not clear from the right side: `int count = Convert.ToInt32(value)`, NOT `var count = Convert.ToInt32(value)`
Use explicit types for foreach loops (the collection name is not enough to know the element type)
Never use var with dynamic — use `dynamic` directly when you want runtime type inference

async-patterns.description: Rules for async/await beyond "always use async". These are patterns that differ between library code and application code.

rules.rule: In library code (NuGet packages, shared utilities): always add ConfigureAwait(false) after every await. This prevents deadlocks when callers have a synchronization context.

In application code (ASP.NET Core, console apps): ConfigureAwait(false) is optional but still recommended for performance. ASP.NET Core does not have a sync context, so deadlocks are not the concern — but it's consistent.
Never block async code with .Result, .Wait(), or GetAwaiter().GetResult() outside of a synchronous entry point. These cause deadlocks in environments with a synchronization context.
DI containers do not support async constructors. Initialize async dependencies in a factory method or by calling an async Initialize() method after construction.
DI factory methods (the Func<IServiceProvider, T> overloads) must be synchronous. Never use .Result inside a DI factory — it causes deadlocks.

di-guidelines.description: Dependency injection rules drawn from official .NET DI guidelines. The basics (constructor injection, no service locator) are in lang-csharp.xml core-principles. These rules cover lifetimes, disposal, and anti-patterns.

lifetime-rules.rule: Singleton: one instance for the lifetime of the application. Use only for stateless services or services with expensive initialization. Must be thread-safe.
Scoped: one instance per request (or per IServiceScope). Use for DbContext, unit-of-work, and per-request state.
Transient: a new instance every time it is resolved. Use for lightweight, stateless services.

Captive dependency: a singleton that holds a scoped or transient service. This is a bug — the shorter-lived service gets promoted to singleton lifetime. Enable scope validation in development: `ValidateScopes = true`.
Never resolve a scoped service from the root IServiceProvider. Only resolve from IServiceScope. Resolving scoped services from root makes them behave as singletons and leaks memory.

disposal-rules.rule: Never call Dispose() on services you received through constructor injection. The container owns the lifetime and calls Dispose() automatically at end-of-scope or shutdown.
Do not register IDisposable instances with transient lifetime — the container holds a reference until it shuts down, leaking memory. Use a factory pattern instead.
Services created with `new` outside the container are NOT disposed automatically. The developer is responsible.

anti-patterns.rule: Service locator: injecting IServiceProvider and calling GetService<T>() at runtime. Use constructor injection instead. Service locator hides dependencies and makes testing harder.
Static access to services: capturing ApplicationServices as a static field. Causes the same lifetime and testability problems as the service locator pattern.
Storing data in the container: the DI container is not a cache or session store. Use IMemoryCache, IDistributedCache, or a scoped service for per-request data.

ef-core-performance.description: EF Core query performance rules. AsNoTracking and materialization are already in lang-csharp.xml guardrails. These rules cover projections, N+1, bulk operations, and pagination.

rules.rule: Project only the columns you need with Select. Loading a full entity when you only need two fields transfers unnecessary data and allocates objects you don't use.

Avoid lazy loading in production code. It looks convenient but triggers one database query per navigation property access, which is the N+1 problem. Use eager loading (Include) or explicit loading instead.
Use Include for eagerly loading related data you know you will need. Combine with filtered Include when you need a subset.
For bulk updates and deletes in EF Core 7+, use ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete. They translate to a single SQL statement and do not load entities into memory.

Always paginate queries that return unbounded result sets. Use Take(n) at minimum; for production, use keyset pagination (WHERE id > lastId ORDER BY id TAKE n) rather than Skip/Take which gets slower as offset grows.
Stream large result sets with AsAsyncEnumerable() instead of ToListAsync() to avoid loading everything into memory at once.

string-and-collections.description: Modern C# syntax for strings and collections. These are patterns the lang-csharp.xml file does not cover.

rules.rule: Prefer raw string literals (triple-quoted) over verbatim strings or escape sequences for multi-line or complex strings
Use string interpolation ($"...") for short concatenation. Use StringBuilder for loops with large text.
Use collection expressions ([...]) for initializing any collection type — available from C# 12
Use language keywords for built-in types: string not String, int not Int32, bool not Boolean
Place using directives outside the namespace declaration to avoid ambiguous name resolution when dependencies introduce conflicting namespace names
Use file-scoped namespace declarations for files with a single namespace

quick-reference.item: Types/methods/properties/constants: PascalCase. Private fields: _camelCase. Params/locals: camelCase. No ALL_CAPS.
Use when type is obvious from right side. Explicit for method return values where type isn't clear. Always explicit in foreach.
Required in library code after every await. Optional but recommended in app code.
.Result and .Wait() cause deadlocks. Async code must stay async all the way up.
DI factory methods must be synchronous. Never call .Result inside AddSingleton/AddScoped factories.
Singleton injecting a scoped/transient = bug. Enable ValidateScopes=true in development.
Never dispose injected dependencies. The container owns their lifetime.
Select() to load only needed columns. Never load a full entity for a read-only display path.
Never iterate navigation properties without Include. Use Include() or explicit loading.
EF Core 7+ bulk operations. Zero entity loads, one SQL statement.
Always paginate unbounded queries. Keyset pagination beats Skip/Take at scale.
